what: Credit Acceptance lends money to people with poor or no credit history so they can buy used cars. It does not deal with borrowers directly: car dealers originate the loans and Credit Acceptance funds them, sharing the collections with the dealer through its portfolio programme.
customers: Subprime used-car buyers, reached through thousands of independent and franchised car dealers across the United States.
money: Interest and fees earned on consumer auto loans funded through dealers.
Ancillary products such as service contracts and GAP insurance, and dealer fees.
moat: Decades of loss data on the riskiest borrowers and a dealer-sharing structure that aligns incentives: dealers are paid from what the loan actually collects, so they have reason to sell cars borrowers can afford.
risks: Loan performance worsens when unemployment rises, and recent loan vintages have collected less than forecast.
Regulators and state attorneys general have sued over its lending practices.
Funding depends on debt markets: it carries $6.4 billion of debt.
opportunities: Heavy buybacks have shrunk the share count dramatically over the past decade.
When banks pull back from subprime lending, Credit Acceptance can write more loans at better terms.
watch: The forecast collection rate on recent loan vintages. Every earnings figure the company reports rests on that forecast, and revisions to it drive the stock.
view: Credit Acceptance is one of the most misunderstood companies on the market, partly by design. Its accounting is unusual, its management says little, and its customers are among the most financially fragile in America. The price-to-free-cash-flow figure of 3.75 is misleading: operating cash flow includes collections on loans that must be replaced by new lending, so it says nothing about cash the business can distribute. The P/E of about 15 is the better guide, and it depends entirely on how much the loans will eventually collect.

That forecast is where the investment lives. The company books income based on its expected collection rate, and in recent years loans written in 2021 and 2022, when used-car prices were at their peak, have collected less than forecast. Each downward revision cuts reported earnings and the value of the loan book. The long record is excellent - the company has been profitable through every recession since the 1990s - but recent vintages have been the weakest in years.

At about $465, with a market value of $4.7 billion, the shares price in a decent probability of further revisions and of regulatory penalties. I respect the business model but would not buy until collection forecasts stop falling; the buybacks are only valuable if the book value they are buying is real. This is a situation where patience costs little and being early can cost a lot.
bull: Collection forecasts stabilise, newer vintages perform, and heavy buybacks at a low multiple compound book value per share.
bear: A weaker job market pushes losses higher on already-soft vintages, regulators impose penalties, and funding costs rise just as the loan book shrinks.
